Car Nut Got 1968 Charger R/T "Family Car," Bounced 8 States in 32 Years, Broadcast Sheet Still in It
49 photos
Photo: YouTube/Mopars5150
Cars staying with one owner, or one family for decades are not unusual. But a car that moves around through eight of the 48 contiguous states of the Union is not something you hear about from your local Amazon delivery guy every week. Or ever. so picture the amazement of this Moparhead when said owners of said car reached out to aske if he’d buy it. Did I mention it’s a numbers-matching 1968 Dodge Charger R/T?
The story begins in 1994 (for some of use, that’s two holidays ago), when a gearhead named Mark found himself home alone in Sacramento, California, during a weekend. The man’s wife together with their two kids left to visit her mother (Mark’s in-law), leaving the man unbothered to solve a simple task he’d been postponing for years: find a good driver car.
Mark already possessed a rocky history with Chrysler products, having previously owned a 1967 Dodge Charger fastback that stranded his wife almost every time she drove it until he finally parted ways with that temperamental machine in the mid-1980s. Mopar ownership experience in a nutshell – back when most Dodge Chargers were simply winter beaters, grocery-getter, dime-a-dozen basket cases that were only marginally good as teen’s first cars.
Browsing the classic car classified ads in the Sacramento Bee newspaper, Mark narrowed his search down to two candidates: a 1979 Ford Mustang hatchback driven gently by an older woman (the ideal candidate) and a 1968 Dodge Charger R/T that had been drag raced. After taking out a high-interest cash advance on his credit card, he still stood $1,000 short of the asking price for the 10-year-newer Mustang and $750 below the seller's asking price for the Dodge.
Photo: YouTube/Mopars5150 His prior experience with Dodge Chargers had left an indelible impression on the family man, who was now a responsible adult with enough sense to make a mature decision for his family. So of course he went all in on the muscle car, leaving the old lady’s fox-body pony Ford for someone else to enjoy. Why live bother-free, when you can always have weekly domestic tornado over a life-altering decision?
Choosing raw horsepower over daily practicality, Mark visited the Charger first and met the owner's father, who was selling the former drag racer to fund his son's medical treatment in a rehabilitation facility. Mark offered every single dollar of borrowed cash he held in his hands. The seller accepted the deal, and Mark drove the big-block muscle car home feeling untouchable, only to find out that you can, in fact, camp indoors, only it’s called “sleeping on the couch.”
At the time of the purchase, Mark worked on the morning broadcast for a Sacramento rock radio station and quickly convinced the station and its commercial advertisers to sponsor a mechanical refresh adventure.
Photo: YouTube/Mopars5150 Through those local promotional partnerships, he rebuilt crucial components of the Charger's 440-cubic-inch Magnum V8 engine. He initially dreamed of executing a full factory-correct restoration, but time and finances transformed the muscle car into a rolling project.
Over the next 26 years, as Mark transitioned into a career in law enforcement and served as a state park warden near El Vado Lake in New Mexico, the Charger followed him nationwide. The Dodge was trailered through California, New Jersey, Texas, New Mexico, Michigan, Pennsylvania, and Vermont. On every move, Mark assured transport drivers the engine would start once the negative battery terminal was connected, yet it never fired up.
While garaging the coupe in Vermont, Mark fired up the big-block a few times each year and changed its motor oil every other year, but he eventually accepted that he would never complete the project. In 2020, before retiring to San Antonio, he passed the Charger to Margaret, his daughter, and Jared, her husband, so it would stay in the family. The couple promptly loaded the classic Mopar onto a trailer and hauled it to Florida.
Photo: YouTube/Mopars5150 Without a personal garage in Florida during their years-and-a-half stay, the couple rented a secure storage unit to shield the Charger from the elements. On weekends, they visited the unit, fired up the 440 V8, took short drives, occasionally smoked the rear tires, and spent hours browsing YearOne and JEGS restoration catalogs. Even while trailering the car to three successive homes across Texas, crowds gathered around it at every fuel stop.
With an upcoming move to Idaho and a later relocation to Northern California on the horizon, Margaret and Jared recognized their weekend routines left no bandwidth for an extensive rebuild. (At this time, I’m beginning to wonder if “Wander” is first nature in this family, or they just can’t grow roots deep enough in one place).
So, they made the reasonable decision: let it go to someone who can actually take care of it. it probably wasn’t as easy as it sounds, given the emotional connection to the car's XS29 VIN stamping. This Charger R/T was assembled at the Hamtramck plant in Michigan near where Margaret's family once resided and where Jared graduated from Wayne State University.
Photo: YouTube/Mopars5150 There are quite a few Texas-based classic car dealerships that would have taken the car off them with both hands, but the couple didn’t just shoot in the dark. They reached out to Mopars5150, after a careful study of alternative. It doesn’t take a rocket science degree to determine that a 1968 Charger R/T with its original engine and transmission will automatically trigger the DEFCON 1 alert level on the YouTubing gearheads. Particularly when they learned the car was just an hour’s drive away.
Arriving at the property, Tony Sedillo inspected the remarkably solid California sheet metal. While the exterior wears weathered paint, a thick blanket of dust, and a replacement hood taken from a yellow donor car, the underside of the trunk lid displays its original factory E1 dark blue finish. Years prior to 1994, an earlier owner filled the circular 1968 side marker lights, installed an alarm cylinder on the fender, and added 1969 rear quarter emblems.
Inside the non-air-conditioned interior, factory bucket seats sit under aftermarket covers alongside a column-shifted 3-speed TorqueFlite automatic, a dashboard clock, and the outboard dash speakers of a rare factory 8-track radio setup. Although the original fender tag disappeared before Mark bought the car, he preserved every factory component he ever unbolted, boxing up the original drums after completing an aftermarket front disc brake conversion to make the Charger safer.
Photo: YouTube/Mopars5150 The previous owner who drag-raced this old classic wanted to perform a 4-speed swap, but fortunately never got to it, and the long-time errant caretaker who got it in ’94 was adamant on keeping it just as it left the assembly line, with its column shifter in place.
After four attempts, the engine fired up, so the YouTuber drove it on the trailer – that’s always a good sign for an old Mopar, and a great thing to have on an iconic muscle car like the 1968 Dodge Charger, the model that propelled the moniker into stardom. The emblematic round taillights and the concealed front lamps made history when they appeared on September 25, 1967, and became downright legendary on October 17, 1968, when “Bullitt” had its first public screening.
The second-generation Charger was allowed into the Road/Track family (established by the Coronet a year before), and it took full advantage of its birth rights. Out of the 96,000+ cars sold, 17,600 were R/Ts. The vast majority came in the standard configuration: 440-4 Magnum V8 (17,109 examples, 14,366 of which were 3-speed Torqueflite automatics), while the 426 Hemi motor was installed in 475 Chargers.
Tony Sedillo, the Mopars5150 know-it-all, went through the car and found the broadcast sheet in the rear seat, confirming that this is what it says it is. If you’re on the lookout for a project Mopar, this car will be available through their Celeste, Texas, showroom.
